nameStory: The Alder Flycatcher gets its name from its love of alder thickets, where it builds its nests and hunts for insects. The scientific name Empidonax comes from ancient Greek meaning 'gnat master,' which perfectly describes this tiny insect-eating champion. Its species name 'alnorum' is simply Latin for 'of the alders,' making this one of the most straightforward bird names around!
description: The Alder Flycatcher is a small, olive-brown bird about the size of a chickadee that specializes in catching flying insects. These compact hunters have grayish-olive backs, whitish bellies with a slight yellow wash, and two pale wing bars that stand out against their darker wings. They're members of the tyrant flycatcher family, known for their aggressive hunting style of darting out from perches to snatch insects mid-flight. Like many small flycatchers, they have a slightly oversized head and a relatively wide, flat bill perfect for their insect-catching lifestyle.

idTips.label: Song
idTips.description: Listen for a distinctive 'fee-BEE-o' or 'free-BEER' call that sounds raspy and emphatic, quite different from other small flycatchers

idTips.label: Wing bars
idTips.description: Look for two prominent white or pale yellow wing bars that contrast nicely against the brownish-olive wings

idTips.label: Eye ring
idTips.description: Notice the thin but distinct white eye ring that gives the bird an alert, wide-eyed appearance

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: The bill appears broad and flat when viewed from the side, perfect for snapping up insects - it looks almost too big for such a small bird

idTips.label: Posture
idTips.description: Sits upright on exposed branches with a characteristic flycatcher stance, ready to dart out after flying insects

habitat: Look for Alder Flycatchers in wet, shrubby areas throughout New England, especially around alder thickets, willow groves, and boggy edges. They prefer areas where water meets dense shrubland - think beaver ponds, stream edges, and wet meadows with scattered bushes. You'll often find them in second-growth areas and forest clearings that stay moist year-round.

seasonality.spring: Arrives in late May and immediately begins singing from prominent perches in alder thickets. Males are very vocal during territory establishment, making this the best time to hear their distinctive calls.
seasonality.summer: Active breeding season with birds constantly hunting insects for their young. Watch for their characteristic fly-catching behavior from mid-level perches in shrubby areas.
seasonality.fall: Becomes much quieter by late August as they prepare for migration. Still present but requires more patience to spot without their frequent calling.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent from New England, having migrated to Central and South America for the winter months.

funFact: Alder Flycatchers were only recognized as a separate species from Willow Flycatchers in 1973 - before that, scientists thought they were the same bird! The breakthrough came when researchers realized their songs were completely different, even though the birds look nearly identical.
confusionNotes: Nearly impossible to distinguish from Willow Flycatcher by sight alone - they're essentially identical twins! The key is voice: Alder Flycatchers say 'fee-BEE-o' while Willow Flycatchers say 'fitz-bew.' Remember: 'Alder' and 'fee-BEE-o' both have three syllables, while 'Willow' and 'fitz-bew' both have two syllables.
contextualKnowledge: The Alder/Willow Flycatcher identification challenge represents one of birding's classic examples of 'sibling species' - birds that look identical but are genetically distinct. This discovery revolutionized how scientists think about bird classification and showed that song can be more important than appearance for species identification.
compareHints: Among the Empidonax flycatchers, Alder Flycatchers are most easily separated by voice rather than appearance. Least Flycatchers have a sharper 'che-BEK' call and are smaller, while Yellow-bellied Flycatchers prefer deeper woods and have a more pronounced yellow belly. The Alder's raspy 'fee-BEE-o' song is really your best bet for positive identification in this tricky genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Empidonax cousins in New England, the Least Flycatcher is noticeably smaller and more compact than Alder and Willow Flycatchers, with a proportionally larger head and shorter bill.
Among New England's Empidonax flycatchers, willow flycatchers are most easily confused with alder flycatchers—voice is the key difference.

Among its Empidonax relatives, the yellow-bellied flycatcher is the only one with truly yellow underparts – Least Flycatchers are grayish-white below, while Alder and Willow Flycatchers are whitish with just a hint of yellow.
Among the Empidonax flycatchers, Acadians are the most olive-green above, while Least Flycatchers are grayer and Yellow-bellied Flycatchers are more uniformly yellowish below.
Compared to other Empidonax flycatchers in New England, the Western Flycatcher has a more distinctly teardrop-shaped eye ring and brighter orange-yellow lower mandible.
Among Empidonax flycatchers, Hammond's shows the most peaked crown and does less tail-flicking than Least Flycatcher.
